title: Global challenges
goals: Add emphasis through inversion after negative adverbs: Never have…, Rarely do…, Not only did… but…, Under no circumstances should…, Little did…
Use inversion also after only, not until and so / such, and recognise which clause is inverted.
Know when it is appropriate (and when it is not) to use inverted structures according to the register.
Talk about the environment and social problems: sustainable, mitigate, inequality, scarcity, accountable.
Propose solutions with precise collocations: tackle, curb, invest in, enforce, raise awareness.
Write a TOEFL-style argumentative essay with a thesis, arguments, a counterargument and a proposal.

learn.title: Inversion after negative adverbs
learn.html:
When a negative or restrictive expression is placed at the start of the sentence for emphasis, the subject and the auxiliary are inverted, just as in a question: I have never seen such a thing → Never have I seen such a thing. If the verb tense has no auxiliary, do / does / did is introduced: Rarely do we see…, Little did they know….

Opening expressionPatternExample
Never / Rarely / Seldom+ auxiliary + subject + verbRarely do governments act before a crisis. / Never have emissions risen so fast.
Hardly / Scarcely … when+ had + subject + past participle … whenHardly had the summit begun when protesters arrived.
No sooner … than+ had + subject + past participle … thanNo sooner had she spoken than the room fell silent.
Not only … (but also)Not only + auxiliary + subject + verb, but … (no inversion in the second part)Not only did the plan fail, but it also widened inequality.
Under no circumstances / On no account / At no point / In no way+ auxiliary (modal) + subject + verbUnder no circumstances should the data be shared.
Little (= barely, not at all)Little + did + subject + base verbLittle did they realise how serious it was.
Nowhere / Not once+ auxiliary or be + subjectNowhere is the damage more visible than in coastal cities.

Nuances. (1) Hardly/Scarcely go with when; No sooner goes with than; mixing them up is a very common mistake. (2) Little did is almost always used with verbs of knowledge or perception (know, realise, imagine, suspect) and usually has a dramatic or ironic tone. (3) If not only modifies an element other than the verb, there is no inversion: Not only the minister but also the mayor resigned.

Register. It is a typical structure of formal written language, speeches and essays; in spontaneous conversation it is rarely heard and can sound theatrical. In an essay, one or two well-placed inversions (for example, to reinforce a key idea) add style; one in every sentence takes away naturalness.

watch.wrong: Rarely we see politicians admit mistakes.
watch.right: Rarely do we see politicians admit mistakes.
watch.why: After the negative adverb, invert with an auxiliary: do + subject + verb.

watch.wrong: No sooner had she arrived when the meeting began.
watch.right: No sooner had she arrived than the meeting began.
watch.why: No sooner goes with than; hardly and scarcely go with when.

watch.wrong: Under no circumstances you should ignore the warning.
watch.right: Under no circumstances should you ignore the warning.
watch.why: Expressions starting with no require inversion: modal + subject.

watch.wrong: Little did they realised the danger.
watch.right: Little did they realise the danger.
watch.why: After did the verb takes the base form, as in any question with did.

learn.title: Only, not until and so / such: more cases of inversion
learn.html:
Inversion is not limited to negative adverbs. It also occurs after only + a time, manner or condition expression, after not until, and in emphatic structures with so … that / such … that.

StructureExampleNote
Only after / when / if / then + clause or phraseOnly after the flood did the council act.The inversion happens in the main clause, not in the when/after clause: Only when she left did he understand.
Only by / through / in this way + -ing or nounOnly by cutting emissions can we avoid the worst effects.Very common in essays when proposing solutions.
Not until … + inverted main clauseNot until the ice melted did scientists grasp the scale of the problem.Equivalent to It was not until… that…; the subject of the main clause goes after the auxiliary.
So + adjective + be + subject + thatSo severe was the drought that crops failed.Very formal; it replaces The drought was so severe that…
Such + be + subject + thatSuch was the scale of the problem that no country could solve it alone.Here such works like an adjective: "such was…".

How to recognise the clause that is inverted. In Not until she arrived did the meeting begin, the subordinate clause (she arrived) keeps its normal word order; the one that is inverted is the main clause (did the meeting begin). A good rule: find the main verb and put the auxiliary before the subject.

Alternative without inversion. Only after the flood did the council act can also be said as The council acted only after the flood: same content, more neutral tone. Inversion adds emphasis and formality.

watch.wrong: Not until she arrived the meeting began.
watch.right: Not until she arrived did the meeting begin.
watch.why: The main clause after not until is inverted with did.

watch.wrong: Only when did he leave the room he realised his mistake.
watch.right: Only when he left the room did he realise his mistake.
watch.why: It is the main clause that is inverted, not the one introduced by when.

watch.wrong: So loud the music was that nobody could talk.
watch.right: So loud was the music that nobody could talk.
watch.why: With so + adjective at the start, be and the subject are inverted.

watch.wrong: Only by acting now we can prevent disaster.
watch.right: Only by acting now can we prevent disaster.
watch.why: Only by + -ing at the start requires inversion: can + subject.

learn.title: Other cases of inversion and when to use them
learn.html:
Besides the patterns above, inversion appears in other formal and literary structures. Recognising them helps you read academic and journalistic texts and choose when to produce them yourself.

  • Inverted conditionals (level review): Had we acted sooner, the damage would have been smaller. / Should you need help, contact us. / Were the targets stricter, emissions would fall.
  • Neither / nor / so + auxiliary + subject: The authorities did not respond; nor did they apologise. / The sea is rising, and so are temperatures. Note: with neither/nor, the verb in the other clause takes an affirmative form.
  • Locative inversion (subject and verb, without an auxiliary): Here comes the evidence. / On the hillside stood a row of abandoned factories. It is used mainly in narratives and descriptions.
  • Formal comparison: The economy grew, as did emissions. (as + auxiliary + subject, in formal comparisons: "and so too…").

When to use it in an essay. Inversion is an emphasis device: use it to underline a key idea (a conclusion, a warning, an essential condition). Two or three well-distributed examples in a 300-word essay add style; if it appears in every sentence, the text sounds artificial and the reader loses the thread. Accuracy matters too: an incorrect inversion (Rarely we see…) costs more than a simple, correct construction would.

For the TOEFL. Examiners value both syntactic variety and accuracy. A safe strategy: master three or four formulas, for example Only by + -ing + can we…, Not only does… but also…, Under no circumstances should… and Rarely has… been…, and apply them where the argument needs more force.

watch.wrong: The sea is rising, and so temperatures are.
watch.right: The sea is rising, and so are temperatures.
watch.why: After so (= also) comes auxiliary + subject.

watch.wrong: The authorities did not respond; nor they apologised.
watch.right: The authorities did not respond; nor did they apologise.
watch.why: Nor requires inversion: nor + auxiliary + subject.

watch.wrong: Not only we must reduce emissions, but we must also adapt.
watch.right: Not only must we reduce emissions, but we must also adapt.
watch.why: After not only at the start, the modal + subject order is inverted.

watch.wrong: Should you will need help, call us.
watch.right: Should you need help, call us.
watch.why: In an inverted should, the verb takes the base form, without will.

learn.title: Strategy: the TOEFL-style argumentative essay
learn.html:
The argumentative essay calls for a clear position, supported by reasons and examples, and a response to objections. For a topic such as "Governments, not individuals, should solve environmental problems", this 4- or 5-paragraph structure (≈ 300 words) works well:

  1. Introduction (3–4 sentences): give context, present the problem and end with the thesis (This essay argues that… / I firmly believe that…). Avoid copying the prompt.
  2. Paragraph 1 – main argument: a topic sentence, the reason, a concrete example and a sentence connecting it to the thesis.
  3. Paragraph 2 – second argument: same structure; use addition connectors (moreover, by the same token).
  4. Paragraph 3 – counterargument and refutation: Critics may argue that… There is some truth in this; nevertheless…
  5. Conclusion: restate the thesis in other words, summarise the arguments and offer a proposal or a projection (Only by… can societies…).

Tips: plan for 3–4 minutes before writing; one idea per paragraph; specific examples (figures, cases) are better than generalities; formal register with no contractions; check agreement, prepositions and any inversion you have used. If you have two minutes left, check only form errors; do not rewrite ideas.

learn.title: Expressions for arguing and proposing solutions
learn.html:
• A growing body of evidence suggests that… — backing a claim with data, in an academic way.
  • It is widely acknowledged that… — presenting a consensus.
  • Critics may argue that…; there is some truth in this, yet… — conceding and refuting.
  • A more effective approach would be to… — proposing an alternative.
  • Only by + -ing can we / can societies… — emphasising an essential condition.
  • Failure to + verb will result in / lead to… — warning about consequences.
  • In the long run / In the short term, … — placing effects in time.
  • Rarely has … been so … / Never before has… — stressing the exceptional with inversion.
  • Taking everything into account, … / On balance, … — closing with an evaluation.

write.prompt: TOEFL-style argumentative essay (300 to 350 words). Topic: 'Some people believe that governments should be mainly responsible for solving environmental problems. Others believe that individuals can make the biggest difference. Which view do you support? Use specific reasons and examples.' Present a clear thesis, develop two arguments with examples, respond to an objection and conclude with a proposal.
targets: inversion after negative adverbs and only / not until
checklist: Introduction with a clear thesis
One paragraph per argument, with a topic sentence and a concrete example
Counterargument acknowledged and refuted (Critics may argue that…; nevertheless…)
At least two correct inversions (Not only does…, Only by… can…, Rarely has…, Under no circumstances should…)
At least three solution collocations (tackle, curb, invest in, enforce, raise awareness…)
Conclusion with a proposal (Only by … can societies…)
Formal register, no contractions, varied connectors
Between 300 and 350 words
write.model:
Environmental problems, from rising sea levels to plastic pollution, are among the most pressing challenges of our age, and the question of who should bear the main responsibility for solving them is hotly debated. Although individual choices matter, I firmly believe that governments should lead the effort, because only they have the power, resources and authority to bring about change on the necessary scale.

The first reason is that governments alone can enforce rules that apply to everyone. Not only does legislation set binding limits on industrial emissions, but it also creates a level playing field, so that responsible companies are not punished for doing the right thing. Consider the international ban on ozone-damaging chemicals agreed in the 1980s: it succeeded largely because it was enforced by national authorities, and the hole in the ozone layer is now slowly healing. Voluntary action by millions of individuals could never have achieved that result so quickly.

The second reason concerns investment. Tackling climate change requires enormous funding for renewable energy, public transport and research. Rarely has a private citizen been able to build a wind farm or electrify a railway network. By contrast, governments can invest in infrastructure that makes sustainable behaviour the easy choice, for example by providing affordable trains that persuade commuters to leave their cars at home.

Critics may argue that individuals ultimately drive demand, and that consumers who change their habits can transform entire markets. There is some truth in this. Nevertheless, personal choices are heavily shaped by the options available, and it is unrealistic to expect people to choose clean alternatives that do not exist or are unaffordable. Individuals can raise awareness and put pressure on politicians, but they cannot replace policy.

Under no circumstances should governments use individual responsibility as an excuse for inaction. Instead, they should curb emissions through taxation, subsidise green technology and educate citizens. Only by combining firm legislation with public engagement can societies protect the planet for future generations.

write.prompt: Second argumentative essay (250 to 300 words). Topic: 'Wealthier countries have a greater responsibility than poorer countries to reduce environmental damage. Do you agree or disagree?' Defend your position, propose at least two solutions and use inversion in moderation.
targets: inversion (Not only, Little did, Hardly… when)
checklist: Clear position from the introduction
Two arguments developed with examples
Two concrete solutions using the vocabulary of the block
One concession (Admittedly / There is some truth in…)
One or two well-placed, correct inversions, without overusing them
Nominalisations or connectors from the previous unit (nevertheless, by the same token, hence)
Conclusion that restates the thesis
Between 250 and 300 words
write.model:
I strongly agree that wealthier countries bear a greater responsibility for reducing environmental damage. This is not a matter of charity but of fairness, since the countries that have contributed most to the problem also have the most resources to address it.

First, wealthy nations are historically responsible for the bulk of greenhouse gas emissions. Having industrialised two centuries ago on coal and oil, they built their prosperity at the expense of the atmosphere, and the cost is now being borne disproportionately by poorer nations. Island states and drought-stricken regions, which have contributed almost nothing to global warming, are the first to suffer its effects. By the same token, it would be unjust to ask them to slow their own development while others continue to consume far more.

Second, richer countries have the capacity to act. Not only can they afford clean technology, but they can also develop it. Hence they should lead in research and share their innovations rather than protect them with patents.

Two solutions seem particularly important. Firstly, wealthier governments should honour their pledges to finance climate adaptation in developing countries, and increase them in line with their emissions. Secondly, they should transfer renewable energy technology at low cost so that poorer economies can skip the polluting stage altogether.

Admittedly, there is some truth in the argument that rapidly growing economies, such as China and India, now produce large quantities of emissions, and they cannot be exempt from all responsibility. Nevertheless, per head of population their emissions remain far below those of the richest nations.

In conclusion, those who have benefited most from polluting should do the most to repair the damage. Only by accepting this principle can the world hope to reach a fair and effective agreement.

reading.title: Thinking globally, acting locally?
reading.intro: Read the essay and answer the questions.
paragraphs: It has become fashionable to say that the world's problems are too large for any individual to solve, and fashionable, too, to answer that every little helps. Both positions contain a grain of truth, yet neither tells us much about how real change happens. Global challenges such as climate change, inequality and the loss of biodiversity are not simply large versions of everyday problems; they are tangled together, and the solution to one often aggravates another.

Take the transition to renewable energy. Few people would dispute that cutting emissions is urgent, and the technology to do so exists. Yet the minerals needed for batteries are mined mostly in poorer countries, often in conditions that harm local communities and ecosystems. Not only does this raise questions of fairness; it also threatens to undermine public support for the transition itself. Rarely is it acknowledged in political speeches that the cleanest option on paper may carry hidden costs elsewhere.

Inequality complicates matters further. Wealthier households produce far more emissions per person than poorer ones, but it is the poor who are most exposed to floods, heatwaves and failed harvests, and who have the fewest resources with which to adapt. Little did the architects of early industrial economies imagine that the benefits of cheap energy would be enjoyed by some while the bill was sent to others. Climate policy that ignores this imbalance risks being not merely unfair but ineffective, because people who feel they are paying for other people's comfort will not support it for long.

What, then, should be done? A growing body of evidence suggests that no single measure will suffice. Carbon pricing can change behaviour, but only if the revenue is used visibly, for instance to protect low-income households from higher bills. Investment in public transport and energy-efficient housing delivers benefits that people can feel within a few years, which matters politically. Conservation works best when local communities are partners rather than obstacles: in several regions, forests managed by the people who live in them have lost less woodland than strictly protected reserves. Such examples show that sustainability is as much a question of governance as of technology.

Critics may argue that these ideas are naive, since governments face short election cycles and powerful industries resist change. There is some force in this objection. Nevertheless, history offers encouraging precedents: the rapid phase-out of ozone-damaging chemicals shows that international cooperation is possible when costs are shared fairly and verification is credible. Not until the evidence became undeniable, however, did governments act, and that delay is itself the lesson. Only by treating prevention as cheaper than repair can societies escape the habit of responding to crises after the damage is done.

None of this absolves individuals. Choices about travel, diet and consumption matter, if only because they shape what is politically acceptable. But the idea that personal virtue can substitute for collective action is, at best, a comforting distraction. The most useful role for individuals may be to demand, vote for and support the large-scale changes that no household can deliver alone.

listening.title: A low-emission zone for the city centre
listening.intro: Listen to the debate at a town council meeting. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. Tonight we're discussing the proposed low-emission zone in the city centre. Councillor Ortiz, would you like to begin?
Thank you. Let me be clear about the problem. Air quality in the centre has exceeded the legal limit on more than ninety days this year. Never before have we recorded figures like these.
The plan is simple: older, polluting vehicles would pay a daily charge, and the revenue would go straight into cheaper buses and cycle lanes.
Thank you. Mr Hale, you run a delivery business. What's your take?

Honestly, I'm torn. Something has to change, I agree, but small firms like mine can't replace a van overnight. Not only would the charge hit our margins, but it would also push prices up for customers.
That's a fair concern, and it's why we're proposing a two-year grace period and grants for cleaner vehicles.
Grants help, but they never seem to cover the full cost. Only when the grant covers at least half the price will most of us be able to switch.
Councillor, is that something the council can do?
We're looking into it. Had we more funding, we'd offer it tomorrow, but there are trade-offs. Under no circumstances do we want to burden the people who can least afford it.
Then why not start with the buses? Fix the service first and people will leave their cars at home voluntarily.
Sensible in theory, but rarely does it work in practice. Not until driving becomes costly do most people try the alternatives. The evidence from other cities is quite consistent.
So the real question is sequencing. Mr Hale, would a phased approach change your view?
It would. If the grace period is genuine and the grants are real, I'd back it. Little did I expect to say that when I walked in, mind you.
Understood. Let's put that on the record and move to a vote after the break.

tasks.prompt: Present your position on a global challenge (climate change, inequality, water scarcity…) and defend it with two reasons.
questions: Which global challenge worries you most?
Who is mainly responsible for dealing with it?
Are you optimistic about the future?
tasks.model: For me, water scarcity is the most pressing challenge, particularly in a country like Mexico. Rarely does it make the headlines until a crisis hits, yet millions of people are already affected. Not only is it a question of health; it also fuels inequality, since the poorest households pay the most for water. In my opinion, responsibility lies mainly with governments, but I'm cautiously optimistic, because awareness is growing.
checklist: Clear thesis (For me… / In my view…)
At least one inversion (Rarely / Not only…)
Two reasons with because / since
Vocabulary of society or the environment

tasks.prompt: Propose three concrete solutions to an environmental or social problem and explain which one would be the most effective.
questions: What would you do first to tackle this problem?
Which measure is the most effective in the long run?
tasks.model: I'd propose three measures. First, governments should invest in public transport and subsidise cleaner vehicles. Second, they should enforce stricter limits on industrial emissions. Third, campaigns should raise awareness among consumers. Only by combining all three can we expect real results. If I had to choose one, I'd say the investment in public transport is the most effective in the long run, since it changes habits and cuts emissions at the same time.
checklist: Collocations from the block (tackle, curb, invest in, enforce…)
Clear order: first, second, third
Only by + -ing + can… or another inversion
Justification of the most effective measure

tasks.prompt: Respond to an objection: someone says 'individual action is pointless because companies cause most pollution'. Concede a point and refute it.
questions: Isn't individual action pointless compared with what companies do?
Don't governments need to act first?
What can ordinary people realistically do?
Do you think things will change?
tasks.model: There is some truth in that: companies and governments are responsible for the bulk of emissions. Nevertheless, individual action is far from pointless. Under no circumstances should we use it as an excuse to wait for others. Our choices shape demand, and, what is more, they influence what voters expect from politicians. So the most effective approach is a combination: personal habits plus pressure on those with power.
checklist: Concession (There is some truth in that…)
Refutation with nevertheless / however
One inversion (Under no circumstances…, Not only…)
Closing with a proposal
